constraints: Sandboxed evaluation and a controlled canary are available.
Assignment and rollback criteria can be recorded.
Quality, safety, latency, and cost can be monitored by cohort.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the model had no tools or side effects and the offline suite covered a deterministic contract, a canary would add less safety evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Universal rollout removes comparison, self-approval is not independent evidence, and disabling tools changes the contract being tested.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a small pilot, thorough evaluation, gradual scaling, A/B testing, and human oversight; the environment and rollback constraints are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Test the model in isolation, assign a canary and control, watch guardrails, and revert when a declared criterion is breached.
details.transfer: Stage changes with isolated evidence, controlled exposure, an independent control, and a reversible rollback boundary.

messages.text: Universal exposure removes the control and expands side-effect risk before live behavior is known.
A model’s explanation is not an independent deployment check.
Removing command behavior tests a different system from the one that will be deployed.
Sandbox evidence limits initial blast radius and the canary observes live behavior.
A control and rollback rule preserve a reversible comparison while the canary is evaluated.

feedback.reason: Sandbox evidence and a small reversible cohort answer different questions; a control and explicit rollback limit the blast radius of tool side effects.

options.text: Run the upgrade in a sandbox first and then expose a small reversible canary cohort with quality, safety, latency, and cost monitoring.
Roll out to every shared environment because the offline score is higher.
Let the model approve its own first deployment after it explains why the change is safe.
Define rollback criteria and preserve a control cohort while the canary runs.
Disable command execution during the canary, even though command behavior is part of the production contract.

prompt: A coding-agent model upgrade beats a small offline suite but can edit files and run commands in shared development environments. Select TWO rollout controls.

constraints: The high-risk category has a stricter safety tolerance.
The experiment retains cohort and transcript evidence.
Latency, cost, and safety are guardrails rather than optional diagnostics.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If B improved quality with no guardrail regression and all categories shared the same risk tolerance, broad rollout could follow the plan.
details.errorCorrection: Averages erase severity, and discarding the recorded evidence prevents diagnosis; resolution alone is not the release contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says A/B tests measure real user outcomes but need transcript review to explain changes, and evaluation layers are complementary.
details.scenarioApplication: Review high-risk transcripts, quantify each guardrail by slice, and modify or limit B until it meets the declared boundaries.
details.transfer: Treat safety and operating commitments as gates around an experimental quality lift, then use slices and transcripts to decide the next change.

messages.text: A global lift cannot veto a safety regression in the category with stricter tolerance.
A composite score can hide a hard guardrail breach.
Restarting discards the cohort and transcript evidence needed to identify the trade-off.

feedback.reason: The headline lift cannot override a high-risk safety regression or violated operating limits; the stored cohort evidence should guide the constrained iteration.

options.text: Ship B because the overall resolution lift is positive and inspect the high-risk category later.
Average quality, latency, cost, and safety into one score and ship if it improves.
Review affected slices and keep safety, latency, and cost as guardrails before rollout.
Rollback both prompts and restart without using the recorded category evidence.

prompt: Prompt B lifts correct claim resolution from 82% to 86% but raises p95 latency 40%, cost 25%, and safety escalations in a high-risk category. Account assignment and category slices are recorded. What should the team do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If randomization is infeasible, use a prespecified quasi-experimental design and state its assumptions and remaining confounding.
details.errorCorrection: An observed production difference is not automatically a treatment effect and is not predictably conservative.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B testing estimates causal effects through controlled assignment; opt-in cohorts can differ before the treatment.
details.scenarioApplication: Randomize eligible users or stable accounts between the current and new style, stratify on important workload segments if needed, and measure resolution plus guardrails.
details.transfer: Separate rollout monitoring from causal evidence when users self-select into a variant.

messages.text: Opt-in users differ by preference and possibly task mix, so the observed difference is not an isolated treatment effect.
Self-selection can bias the comparison in either direction; it does not establish that the observed lift is conservative.
Task mix, time, learning, and other contemporaneous changes can still explain a before/after difference.

feedback.reason: The beta comparison is observational and preference-driven. Treat it as a hypothesis, then randomize or otherwise create a credible comparable counterfactual before attributing the lift to the style.

options.text: The style caused a 9-point lift because the beta group used it in production.
Treat beta results as observational; run randomized assignment before claiming causal lift.
Ship the style to everyone because self-selection only makes the estimate conservative.
Compare only the beta users’ results before and after opt-in to remove user preference effects.

prompt: A new answer style is released to users who opt into a beta because they already prefer detailed responses. Their resolution rate is 9 points higher than the default group; no random assignment or pre-release matched evaluation exists. What can the team conclude?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The product owner can authorize a new cost ceiling only through a new decision basis; the current experiment cannot infer that change.
details.errorCorrection: Do not average the arms or mine an unplanned subgroup to make a guardrail failure disappear.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B decisions must respect declared guardrails across quality, safety, latency and cost; a favorable primary outcome does not automatically waive a constraint.
details.scenarioApplication: Report treatment and control estimates by assigned arm, show the $0.78 cost against the $0.50 ceiling, and preserve safety results as a separate measure.
details.transfer: Apply the complete predeclared adoption rule after estimating each outcome.

messages.text: The variant violates the explicit $0.50 cost guardrail even though one outcome improved.
Post hoc selection creates an unplanned subgroup and does not establish that it meets the cost rule.
Averaging treatment and control cost does not change the candidate arm’s measured cost.

feedback.reason: The treatment improves resolution but exceeds the experiment’s adoption cost ceiling. Record both outcomes and do not adopt it under this rule.

options.text: Adopt the variant because resolution improved and safety did not worsen.
Adopt only for accounts with the largest resolution lift, selecting that slice after reviewing the results.
Keep the candidate behind the predeclared cost ceiling; evaluate resolution and cost together.
Average the old and new cost per case to $0.59 and compare that with the $0.50 ceiling.

prompt: A prompt variant improves successful resolution from 80% to 84% on the assigned accounts. It also raises cost per resolved case from $0.40 to $0.78; the experiment plan says the variant is adoptable only if cost stays at or below $0.50 and the safety guardrail holds. Safety is unchanged. What result should be recorded?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If interactions are unlikely or capacity is limited, a predeclared staged design may be simpler, but it estimates fewer interactions at each step.
details.errorCorrection: Do not credit one component based on cost, recency, or a favorable aggregate when all components changed together.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Causal attribution requires variation that separates the candidate explanations; increasing the sample for an unchanged bundle does not do that.
details.scenarioApplication: Use a factorial or staged design that preserves a control and varies model, prompt and retrieval in interpretable combinations, while holding the eligible workload and guardrails constant.
details.transfer: Design the next experiment to distinguish the causal claims the release owner needs.

messages.text: Cost and timing do not isolate which intervention caused the observed result.
A larger sample estimates the bundled treatment more precisely but still cannot attribute its effect to one component.
Changing one component at a time can test retrieval’s contribution, but the remaining pair stays confounded and the plan must preserve a comparable control.

feedback.reason: The observed experiment estimates the bundled release, not the contribution of its three simultaneous changes. A controlled multi-arm or factorial follow-up is needed for component attribution.

options.text: Credit the model because it was the most expensive change and the launch metric improved.
Keep all three changes and rerun the same two-arm test with twice as many accounts.
Roll back retrieval only and attribute any remaining lift to the model and prompt together.
Use a controlled or factorial follow-up to attribute effects among the three interventions.

prompt: A rollout analysis shows a 6-point lift after three changes shipped together: a new model, a prompt rewrite, and a different retrieval index. The release was assigned by account, but the owner asks which change caused the lift. What experiment should come next?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the target mix has little or no support in one arm, statistical reweighting cannot create missing counterfactual evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Do not infer comparability from equal totals or drop an inconvenient stratum after seeing outcomes.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization should produce comparable treatment exposure; workload and time imbalance can distort the measured effect, especially for latency.
details.scenarioApplication: Check overlap by time and document length, estimate within-stratum effects and a prespecified target-weighted result, and improve random assignment or blocking for a clean follow-up.
details.transfer: Compare variants under the same workload population and expose residual mix imbalance.

messages.text: Equal account counts do not balance a workload dimension that is strongly associated with treatment timing and latency.
Removing cases after observing imbalance changes the comparison and may leave no comparable target population.
The differing long-document mix and time period confound the prompt effect.

feedback.reason: Account counts alone do not make the arms comparable when exposure periods and document lengths differ. Analyze comparable strata under a declared target mix and rerun if the observed data lack overlap.

options.text: Compare the two raw aggregate means because account counts are equal.
Balance and report document-length workload by arm, then estimate lift on comparable exposures.
Drop weekend requests from the control group and compare only weekday means.
Attribute the weekend latency to the control prompt because those requests were assigned there.

prompt: A prompt A/B test assigns accounts equally, but treatment accounts are mostly evaluated during weekday mornings and control accounts during weekend nights. Long documents are much more common on weekends, and the new prompt changes long-document latency. Which analysis best repairs the comparison?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A valid predeclared sequential design may permit interim decisions, but its boundary must exist before inspecting outcomes.
details.errorCorrection: A nominal p-value does not erase unplanned selection or become confirmatory when reported after the fact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B inference depends on the analysis and stopping plan; repeated testing can inflate false-positive risk.
details.scenarioApplication: Record every metric check, variant tried and stopping point, then preregister a primary outcome, guardrails, multiplicity approach and stopping rule for the confirmatory run.
details.transfer: Disclose exploratory iteration and separate it from a confirmatory causal decision.

messages.text: Repeated looks across metrics and variants increase the chance of finding a nominal result by chance.
Relabeling the chosen result after seeing it does not undo the unplanned comparisons or stopping.
Continuing to peek without a defined rule preserves the same multiplicity and stopping bias.

feedback.reason: The observed result followed repeated unplanned looks across metrics and variants. It can generate a hypothesis but does not support a confirmatory win; use a new prespecified design.

options.text: Declare a win because at least one metric crossed the usual significance line.
Select the variant with the strongest observed metric and report the other results as exploratory without qualification.
Use the predeclared stopping rule or adjust for repeated looks across metrics and variants.
Continue testing until all five metrics are significant, then stop without revising the plan.

prompt: During a live test, an analyst checks five quality metrics every day for two weeks. The team stops the test the first day one metric is nominally significant, after also trying three prompt variants; no interim or multiple-comparison rule was specified. What should be reported?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If persistent assignment is operationally impossible, measure and report carryover explicitly and avoid a clean causal claim until a valid design is available.
details.errorCorrection: More weeks or account-level adjustment cannot identify the prompt effect when the prior treatment changes the next period’s behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Crossover comparisons rely on treatment effects not persisting into later control periods; durable state can violate that assumption.
details.scenarioApplication: Use persistent account assignment for a parallel test, or demonstrate a washout that clears the memory before comparing periods; keep outcomes and guardrails prespecified.
details.transfer: Check whether treatment changes durable user, agent, or system state before selecting a crossover experiment.

messages.text: The same account is not an unaffected control after the B-specific rule remains in memory.
A fixed effect controls stable account differences, not treatment-induced state that carries into the next period.
The state change may explain some outcome, but the alternating design cannot separate that effect from prompt assignment.

feedback.reason: The treatment persists into later control periods, so the alternating comparison mixes prompt assignment with learned workspace state. The within-account design does not remove that carryover.

options.text: Treat the 5-point difference as causal because each account serves as its own control.
Keep alternating and add account fixed effects; the persistent memory averages out across enough weeks.
Model carryover or use a washout; alternating periods do not erase learned workspace rules.
Attribute the entire 5-point lift to prompt B because the memory was introduced during its weeks.

prompt: A support agent test alternates the same accounts between prompt A and prompt B each week to control for account differences. Prompt B teaches a persistent workspace memory to include a new escalation rule; during the following A week, that memory remains active. The measured B weeks show a 5-point resolution lift. What can the team conclude and test next?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cluster randomization may require more teams or longer enrollment; if only twelve teams are available, describe the estimate as limited rather than using an artificially narrow account-level interval.
details.errorCorrection: A large account count cannot repair a small number of treatment clusters or remove shared-playbook spillover.
details.mechanismOrProperty: When treatment is delivered through a shared team environment, outcomes within a team are correlated and can contaminate individual-level assignment.
details.scenarioApplication: Assign whole teams, increase the number of independent teams according to a prespecified power plan, and analyze the randomized cluster while reporting account outcomes and safety guardrails.
details.transfer: Choose the randomization unit to match the smallest shared environment where treatment can spread.

messages.text: A large number of accounts does not increase the number of independent team-level assignments.
Preference-based assignment can confound treatment with supervisor and team differences.
Putting both prompts in the playbook lets treatment cross the same shared boundary the design must control.

feedback.reason: Shared coaching and playbooks let treatment information spill across accounts within a team, so 2,400 account rows do not provide 2,400 independent treatment assignments. Randomize and analyze at the cluster where interference occurs, with enough clusters to estimate the effect.

options.text: Keep account-level assignment and retain the account-level interval because the number of accounts is large.
Randomize and analyze at team level because coaching crosses account boundaries.
Assign every team the prompt that its supervisor prefers and adjust for team in a regression.
Randomize by account, but move examples from both prompts into every team’s playbook so agents can choose the best instruction.

prompt: A company randomizes 2,400 customer accounts across two assistant prompts, but each arm has only six support teams. Every team shares a response playbook and supervisors coach agents using examples from their assigned prompt. The analysis treats all accounts as independent and reports a narrow confidence interval. Which redesign best supports a causal comparison?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A predeclared interim method can support a decision only if it accounts for follow-up censoring and the outcome policy; otherwise wait for the full horizon.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat unobserved follow-up as no reopening, and do not assume the subset with completed follow-up is representative.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Outcome maturity is distinct from sample-size completion; an assigned case that has not yet reached the observation horizon is not a confirmed no-event outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Report the handling-time and same-session results as interim findings, continue follow-up, and evaluate the 30-day reopen rate with the prespecified censoring or missingness method before applying the guardrail.
details.transfer: Align release claims with when each outcome becomes observable, not only when enrollment reaches its target.

messages.text: The required 30-day safety outcome is still unobserved for most assigned accounts, so immediate gains cannot establish that guardrail.
An account that has not completed 30 days is censored, not a confirmed case without a reopening.
The matured subset may differ by assignment or account characteristics; analyze follow-up selection before treating it as the full randomized comparison.

feedback.reason: The primary count and immediate metrics do not establish a 30-day guardrail when most assigned accounts have not reached the outcome window. Preserve the favorable interim evidence and defer the release claim until the prespecified outcome is mature or analyzed under a valid missing-follow-up plan.

options.text: Ship because the planned sample and both immediate outcomes meet the success goal.
Wait for mature safety outcomes or apply the prespecified valid censoring analysis before release.
Count every account without an observed reopening as a no-reopen success, including accounts whose follow-up window is not complete.
Discard the randomized comparison and use only the 40% with mature follow-up, without checking whether follow-up completion differs by arm or account type.

prompt: A randomized support-assistant test reaches its planned account count. The new prompt reduces median handling time by 12% and raises same-session resolution by 3 points. The release contract also limits 30-day case reopenings to at most a 1-point increase, but only 40% of assigned accounts have completed the 30-day follow-up. What conclusion is justified now?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If delivery failures are concentrated in a meaningful segment, report that operational limitation and test the delivery path before broad rollout.
details.errorCorrection: A received-treatment comparison or excluding noncompliers can lose the protection of random assignment; crossover also does not erase the primary evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization identifies an assignment-based effect; conditioning on post-assignment exposure can introduce selection if delivery failures relate to account or outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Estimate outcomes by assigned arm, disclose the 8% and 3% crossover rates and their patterns, then prespecify a secondary exposure analysis if its assumptions are justified.
details.transfer: Preserve the randomized estimand and make treatment receipt a measured implementation outcome.

messages.text: Actual exposure may differ for reasons related to the outcome, so comparing by receipt abandons the randomized assignment.
Removing noncompliers conditions on a post-assignment event and can bias the comparison.
Crossover weakens separation but does not automatically erase the primary evidence.

feedback.reason: The product question concerns assignment to the new policy. The randomized groups preserve that comparison even with imperfect delivery; crossover must be measured and can qualify interpretation, not silently redefine who was randomized.

options.text: Compare outcomes by the prompt each account actually received and discard assignment logs.
Use assignment-based intention-to-treat; report crossover and qualify exposure-based analysis separately.
Remove all accounts that did not receive their assigned prompt and treat the remaining users as randomized.
Declare no effect because any crossover invalidates all information from a randomized test.

prompt: A randomized assistant test assigns 1,000 accounts to prompt B and 1,000 to prompt A. Delivery logs show 8% of B assignments fell back to A, and 3% of A assignments accidentally received B. The product asks whether assigning the new policy improves resolution. Which primary analysis and follow-up are most defensible?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If some outcomes remain unavailable, report their rates and use a predeclared missing-data sensitivity analysis rather than asserting the observed complete-case lift is causal.
details.errorCorrection: A balanced assignment log does not repair a biased analysis table; post hoc weights or complete-case restriction can hide the selection mechanism.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization protects a comparison only for the randomized population and a valid outcome analysis; post-assignment filtering can create differential selection.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the immutable assignment log to rebuild eligible arm counts, trace why 1,100 more treatment sessions were excluded, and evaluate missing outcomes under the prespecified plan.
details.transfer: Audit assignment, exposure, eligibility, and outcome capture as separate stages before reading an experiment estimate.

messages.text: The published table no longer contains the full assigned population, and its arm-specific exclusions may bias the estimate.
Matching row counts after the fact does not explain why treatment outcomes are missing or restore randomized comparability.
Complete transcripts may be missing differently by arm; discarding assignment information makes the selection harder to diagnose.

feedback.reason: The analysis population no longer reflects the balanced randomized cohort, and the differential loss may be related to treatment or outcome. Diagnose the changed denominator before interpreting the apparent lift.

options.text: Report treatment’s observed rate because randomized assignment was originally balanced.
Restore the prespecified denominator by assignment, audit arm-specific session loss, then rerun the analysis.
Reweight the smaller treatment table until its count matches control, then publish the same estimate.
Drop assignment logs and compare only the sessions with complete transcripts.

prompt: An experiment assigns 10,000 eligible accounts to each prompt. The immutable assignment log is balanced, but the analysis table contains 8,900 control accounts and 7,200 treatment accounts after filtering for completed sessions. Treatment has the higher observed resolution rate. The filter was added during the test and no missing-session audit was run. What should the analyst do before interpreting the lift?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fallbacks weaken treatment separation without automatically eliminating all randomized evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Dropping or reassigning accounts conditions on post-assignment events and can bias the result.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of assignment under observed delivery, including noncompliance.
details.scenarioApplication: An exposure-based analysis may be informative but needs separate assumptions and labeling.
details.transfer: Keep assignment, delivery, and actual exposure distinct in experiment reporting.

messages.text: Actual receipt follows a post-assignment fallback and is no longer the randomized comparison; adjustment does not preserve assignment balance.
Excluding noncompliers after assignment can select different populations across arms and biases the primary estimate.
Noncompliance weakens exposure interpretation but the assignment-based result remains informative when delivery is reported and qualified.

feedback.reason: Filtering or reassigning after randomization changes the comparison population. Assignment-based analysis preserves the initial randomized estimate while delivery failure is reported separately.

options.text: Analyze by randomized assignment, report delivery compliance by arm, and qualify any exposure-based analysis separately.
Report an as-treated comparison as primary, grouping accounts by the prompt they actually received and adjusting for the fallback rate.
Keep accounts in their original arms but remove the 17% fallback cases from the denominator, then compare the remaining randomized users.
Pause interpretation until delivery is repaired, because the exposure problem prevents any useful estimate from this randomized assignment.

prompt: A randomized test assigns equal numbers of accounts to A and B. Delivery logs show 17% of B accounts received A after a fallback, while the analyst’s table compares only accounts that received their assigned prompt. What should the primary result report?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The rubric itself affects measurement and should be held constant or evaluated as an explicit factor.
details.errorCorrection: Post-hoc reviewer intuition does not replace a controlled comparison.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Causal attribution requires separating changes or deliberately estimating their combined effects under a design that supports it.
details.scenarioApplication: A larger test of the same bundle can estimate the bundle’s effect but cannot identify which component caused it.
details.transfer: Use a planned design to distinguish interacting changes.

messages.text: A larger sample can estimate the bundled effect more precisely but cannot identify which component caused it.
The comparison still leaves retrieval and evaluator changes entangled with the prompt effect.
Expert judgment can prioritize hypotheses but does not isolate causal contributions among changes deployed together.

feedback.reason: The observed result combines three simultaneous changes, so a larger sample alone cannot attribute the gain to one of them.

options.text: Repeat the combined release with more accounts and use a larger sample to determine whether the joint change reliably improves resolution.
Restore the prior evaluator, keep the new retrieval, and compare the prompt rollback with the combined release on fresh cases.
Ask reviewers to rank the prompt, retrieval, and rubric changes by plausibility, then test the highest-ranked explanation first.
Run controlled comparisons that vary prompt, retrieval, and rubric factors separately or in a planned factorial design.

prompt: A launch report attributes a 5-point resolution gain to a new prompt. The same deployment also changed retrieval ranking and the evaluator’s partial-answer rubric; no previous run tested those changes separately. What follow-up best isolates the cause?

constraints: Account assignment is stable.
The owner can extend the run under the analysis plan.
The sample target, confidence rule, and stopping boundary were predeclared.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A completed planned sample with stable guardrails and a prespecified stopping rule could support rollout from the observed effect.
details.errorCorrection: A point estimate, a premature no-difference conclusion, or changing the stopping rule after seeing data turns noise into policy.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that A/B tests measure real outcomes but are slower and need transcript review; the sample and stopping rules are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve assignment and analysis, collect the planned sample, monitor guardrails by account type, and review transcripts before declaring a winner.
details.transfer: Respect the evidence and stopping rule declared before an experiment, especially when safety coverage is incomplete.

messages.text: A positive early estimate may be noise in an incomplete sample.
Overlapping confidence does not itself define the required stopping decision.
Changing the rule after observing the result invalidates the planned evidence boundary.

feedback.reason: An underpowered and uneven sample does not meet the declared evidence rule; continue under the plan or stop for a specified safety breach.

options.text: Ship the new variant because the early point estimate is positive.
Stop the experiment and declare no difference because the confidence range overlaps.
Continue under the sample plan or stop for a defined safety breach; inspect slices.
Change the stopping rule now so the positive estimate can be used for rollout.

prompt: An A/B test reports a 2% resolution lift after one day, but its predeclared sample target is not met, the confidence range overlaps, and guardrail data is sparse across account types. What decision is justified?

constraints: Exposure, account segment, session, and outcome logs are available.
The original plan requires clean account assignment and comparable segment mix.
The causal effect is needed before changing exposure.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If crossover were absent, segment mix matched the plan, and the sample met the analysis rule, the observed lift could proceed to the predeclared decision.
details.errorCorrection: Weighting cannot recover users who saw both variants or repair a changed exposure mechanism; an unadjusted or premium-only rollout compounds the confound.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes A/B testing as controlling for confounds and requiring sufficient traffic and transcript review; crossover and segment balance are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Use logs to quantify contamination, correct the routing and segment filter, preserve a clean cohort, and rerun before changing exposure.
details.transfer: Audit treatment exposure and population composition before interpreting a live comparison as causal.

messages.text: Weighting cannot restore the missing counterfactual for users exposed to both variants.
A large contaminated sample remains causally invalid.
Selecting the segment that received more favorable exposure turns the composition confound into a rollout rule.

feedback.reason: Crossover and changed composition contaminate treatment exposure and the counterfactual, so the apparent lift is not a valid causal comparison.

options.text: Post-hoc weight the aggregate results by segment and ship B if the adjusted estimate remains positive across the contaminated sessions.
Discard the logs and use the unadjusted lift because the sample is large.
Ship only to premium accounts, where B has the largest observed lift.
Audit crossover and segments, restore account assignment, and rerun before changing exposure.

prompt: Variant B reports a 4-point resolution lift. Account-level assignment was intended, but a routing bug sent 12% of users both variants; B also received twice as many easy premium accounts after a segment filter changed. Logs preserve crossover and composition. What should happen?

constraints: The registered interim time, sample size, primary metric, uncertainty rule, guardrails, assignment log, and analysis output are immutable and available before the result is reviewed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the interim rule were absent, the sample/uncertainty boundary unmet, or a safety guardrail breached, the experiment would continue or stop for the breach rather than declare this interim result.
details.errorCorrection: The first ignores an authorized stopping boundary; the second ignores the registered analysis and creates the unplanned-peeking problem covered by the rejected path. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a small pilot, infrastructure for A/B testing, human feedback, and ongoing updates to offline evaluations from production data. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Apply the registered interim rule, stop or advance exposure as it specifies, preserve the analysis and guardrail evidence, and report the decision as an interim-boundary outcome rather than an unplanned peek.
details.transfer: Use a prespecified stopping rule as the decision boundary and label the evidence according to the stage at which it was collected.

messages.text: The final sample target is not a prerequisite when the registered interim rule is met; waiting changes the declared decision point instead of applying it.
A dashboard result without the registered rule recreates the unplanned-peeking problem.
Resetting discards a valid prespecified boundary instead of applying the documented stopping decision.

feedback.reason: Apply the registered interim rule, stop or advance exposure as it specifies, preserve the analysis and guardrail evidence, and report the decision as an interim-boundary outcome rather than an unplanned peek. The decisive constraint is A prespecified interim rule with sufficient evidence permits the declared decision; the absence of the final sample target alone does not require continuing when the rule authorizes stopping.

options.text: Complete the full sample target before applying the interim rule, so the study is not stopped on partial data.
Apply the registered interim rule, stop or advance as specified, preserve the analysis and guardrail evidence, and label the result as interim.
Declare a winner from the dashboard without applying the registered interim rule or preserving its analysis record.
Reset the experiment and collect a new sample because any decision before the final target is necessarily invalid.

prompt: An A/B test has a predeclared interim analysis at 1,000 eligible accounts, a stopping rule for a large reliable lift, and a safety guardrail. At the interim point, the sample target for the full study is not complete, but the predeclared lift and guardrails meet the documented decision boundary. What should the experiment owner do at this interim point?

constraints: The playbook revision history, account assignment, agent exposure logs, and outcome transcripts are available; users in each arm can interact with the same support staff.

Exposure logs show that the same staff continue using the learned Variant B instruction across account assignments after the shared document is changed; changing the document alone does not remove staff-carried exposure.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If playbooks and agent exposure were isolated by arm, account-level randomization could support the existing A/B decision with the planned transcript review.
details.errorCorrection: The shared playbook makes both cohorts partially treated, so the observed lift cannot be attributed to B and could conceal harm in the intended control. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says A/B tests measure real user outcomes but need transcript review to explain metric changes; multiple evaluation layers are complementary. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Freeze and audit the shared playbook, quarantine and label contaminated observations, remove or version the cross-arm instruction, then rerun a controlled comparison with arm-specific cluster or agent assignment or an explicit residual-interference model.
details.transfer: Check the exposure path, not just assignment, whenever an operational artifact can cross experimental arms.

messages.text: The shared playbook partially treats both arms, so balanced assignment cannot identify B’s effect.
Relabeling both arms does not recover a control group or explain the spillover.
Removing the contaminated observations discards the exposure evidence and can hide harm in the intended control.
Required control: Freeze and audit the shared playbook; quarantine and label contaminated observations, remove or version the cross-arm instruction, and record exposure evidence before the rerun.

Required control: Rerun a controlled comparison with arm-specific cluster or agent assignment because the same staff carry learned Variant B behavior across accounts, or fit an explicit residual-interference model.

feedback.reason: Freeze and audit the shared playbook, quarantine and label contaminated observations, remove or version the cross-arm instruction, then rerun a controlled comparison with arm-specific cluster or agent assignment or an explicit residual-interference model. The same support staff carry learned Variant B behavior across accounts, so no single control restores a valid comparison by itself.

options.text: Keep account-level assignment and credit Variant B because both cohorts received the same support volume.
Freeze and audit the shared playbook; quarantine and label contaminated observations, remove or version the cross-arm instruction, and record exposure evidence before the rerun.
Treat both cohorts as exposed to B and compare their aggregate outcomes without changing the assignment design.
Exclude support interactions from the analysis and infer the treatment effect from the balanced account logs alone.
Rerun a controlled comparison with arm-specific cluster or agent assignment because the same staff carry learned Variant B behavior across accounts, or fit an explicit residual-interference model.

prompt: A/B assignment is account-level, but support agents use one shared response playbook that contains Variant B's new instruction for both cohorts. details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For a deterministic offline formatter with no user impact or side effects, a live randomized cohort would add little evidence.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a report were an unverified anecdote with no reproducible input, investigate it before adding it as an evaluation case.
